summaries.summary: Sentiment analysis uncovers emotion in information, supports political and marketing purposes, product acceptance and feedback systems, and requires sentiment labels defined in a lexicon.
Lexicon acquisition labels information elements by class, usually emotion, and lexicon quality directly affects sentiment classification accuracy.
Lexicon acquisition and sentiment classification can be automatic or manual, including crowdsourcing, which is widely used for polarity lexicons but rarely beyond polarity.
Sentiment analysis commonly uses polarity, distinguishing positive and negative emotion for agreement, disagreement, acceptance, or disapproval toward candidates and products.
Beyond polarity, or pure emotion, sentiment analysis uncovers exact emotions based on emotional theories and can improve several applications with distinct emotion lexicons.
Beyond polarity lexicons rely on strict rules and expert evaluation, use a single emotion per term, and face uniformity, freedom, cost, scalability, and comprehensiveness problems.
This paper presents a multiclass scalable crowdsourced pure emotion lexicon (PEL) based on Plutchik's eight basic emotions, with crowd-identified linguistic elements and worker filtering.
Ekam et al. proposed six basic emotions, while Plutchik added trust and anticipation and presented a circumplex model defining contradictions and combinations.
Sentiment analysis classifies information by conveyed emotion and is separated into polarity and beyond polarity according to the number of classes/emotions required.
Polarity sentiment analysis defines positive and negative states, often with neutral, and may use levels known as fine grained sentiment analysis.
Beyond polarity, or pure emotion, sentiment analysis uses a wider range of specific emotion classes such as sadness, boredom, joy, surprise, anger, fear, and disgust.
Lexicon acquisition can be manual or automatic, but natural language subjectivity inhibits automated methods, leading researchers to manual annotation, established lexicons, or combined approaches.

Crowdsourcing can remove manual lexicon acquisition constraints, with MTurk used for polarity lexicons, one thousand tweets, ten thousand terms, ninety five emoticons, and one thousand four hundred terms.
Sentiment classification occurs at phrase/sentence/submission level, aggregates labeled term emotions, and can be automated or performed manually.
Term and phrase sentiment are main classification inputs; manual classification achieves high relevance but lacks scalability, while automated processes are scalable with lower relevance.
The approach aims at an end to end automated work-flow for pure emotion lexicon creation, evaluation, and enrichment, with pre-processing and crowdsourcing components.

Pre-processing uses tokenization, stemming, and spell check, while crowdsourcing annotates database entries, filters answers, updates valid entries, and evaluates annotations against expert linguists.
During January 2017, a keyword based crawl collected Europe subreddit articles and comments and Twitter tweets containing "Brexit" to capture emotional diversity.
The crawl collected one hundred Reddit articles, more than forty thousand comments, and more than three thousand tweets, storing location, time, upvotes, re-tweets, and favourites.
The corpus had 30227 unique terms; 19193 were validated and 11034 invalidated using the enchant python library and Great British English dictionary.
After validation, Porter Stemming Algorithm identified 10953 distinct term groups, including stop-words, intensifiers, and negators, with unsupervised validation and stemming.
The CrowdFlower task asked contributors to label term groups as emotion, intensifier, or none, without a golden standard, rules, or participation restrictions.
Each of the eleven main-class options is a "subclass"; stem-based term groups have majority main annotations and nonmajority sub annotations, with every annotation logged.
The task interface was refined through experiments by simplifying the question, including only three main classes, and replacing positive and negative with amplifying and weakening.
Contributors choose among three options, specify eight basic emotions, Amplifying or Weakening, or None, with each term group linked to an English dictionary.
More than one hundred eighty contributors performed eighty thousand annotations, with a 660 unique annotation limit, 15% and 85% splits, and mean and median annotations of 429 and 580.
Experiments identified 136 assessment term groups testing emotion evoking, intensifying context, and none, with more than ten thousand annotations analysed separately.
Workers had to properly annotate 80% of assessment term groups within dominant classes, not subclasses, to contribute and get paid.
The paragraph defines workers, eleven subclasses, and the number of total annotations for each worker, followed by DISPLAYFORM0.
The paragraph defines worker sets in the assessment and acquisition processes and gives DISPLAYFORM0 DISPLAYFORM1 for INLINEFORM4.
The paragraph states "and: DISPLAYFORM0 DISPLAYFORM1".
The optimal INLINEFORM0 is found for INLINEFORM1, and the optimal filtering percentage for this study was 40%, INLINEFORM2.
Workers from India and Venezuela contributed 92% of the task and annotated more than 30% of term groups with joy, unlike several countries with more than 300 annotations.
Analysis found workers with large fractions in a single subclass, such as one worker annotating 99% as joy, while existing spamming solutions require gold standards or objective tasks.
Without a gold standard, the authors use a filter relying on annotations and assessment to flag dishonest workers above a single-subclass percentage and discard their annotations.
Before implementing the filter, the authors analysed its effect on eligible workers, with Figure FIGREF22 showing assessment and lexicon acquisition percentages.
Higher single annotation percentages indicate more certain spamming, with similar exclusion rates overall and reduced assessment exclusions due to cautious behaviour on known test questions.
Each assessment term group was annotated more than 120 times by 187 annotators, providing a critical mass of contributors and valuable task findings.
Workers rarely clicked the dictionary link, with less than 0.2% clicking on average, likely causing emotional words such as "vehement, halcyon" to be annotated as none.
Intensifiers are understandable but require critical mass, as initial emotion annotations for "reduce, little, plethora" shifted toward weakening weakening intensifying after tens of annotations.
All words should be evaluated because words and emotions acquire new links, as "anti, serious" were annotated as fear evoking with great emotional diversity.
PEL was created after 40% single annotation filtering, retaining 22 thousand annotations for 9737 term groups from more than seventy thousands annotations for 10593 term groups.
After filtering, joy is dominant and disgust least annotated, with 148 intensifiers, 43 negators, 6801 none terms, and the full lexicon on github.
Workers identified mostly valid intensifiers and negators, but annotations indicate room for improvement in the intensifier class description and examples.
Stemming halved cost and time, while 21% and 20% of term groups had subclass and emotional agreement, and 8.6% showed contradicting or multi-emotion agreement.
The paragraph defines a term group, eleven subclasses, annotation counts, emotion subclass annotations, intensifying subclass annotations, and none annotations.
Each INLINEFORM0 can have a monotonically increasing finite sequence INLINEFORM1 with INLINEFORM2, where DISPLAYFORM0.
Term group INLINEFORM0 has subclass agreement if and only if DISPLAYFORM0.
INLINEFORM0 has emotional agreement if and only if there is subclass agreement with sequence INLINEFORM1 and DISPLAYFORM0.

Subclass agreement means equal annotations between emotional and non-emotional subclasses or multiple non-emotional subclasses, while emotional agreement means equal annotations among multiple emotion subclasses.
Subclass agreement negatively correlates with term-group size, is highest for two-term groups with exactly two subclasses, and indicates stemming didn't confuse workers.
Emotional agreement appeared in 10% of term groups, subclass agreement in 20%, joy was most common, and 697 emotional agreeing term groups of 1434 terms had exactly two emotions.
Dyadic emotional agreements may be interpreted as complex emotions or further annotated, and emotional agreement occurrences decrease as annotations increase.
The lexicon features 17740 annotated terms with 3 classes and 11 subclasses, including 7030 emotion, 191 intensifying, 6801 none, and 3718 subclass agreement terms.
Single annotation reliability agreement measures agreement for term groups with a majority in exactly one sub class and was low in the lexicon.
Based on Fleiss Kappa BIBREF30 and Table TABREF35, term groups with 2 annotations had lowest reliability, while 6 annotations had highest.
Restricting the lexicon to emotions increases reliability for any number of annotators except two, due to fewer possible categories.
Expert and crowd contributors are compared for 1000 term groups, with two Ph.D. linguists and Crowdflower contributors, and expert costs equal nineteen contributors.
Evaluators saw annotation summaries such as "inequality inequity" with 50.0% sadness, 33.33% disgust, 16.67% anger, and rated validity from 1 to 5.
Figure FIGREF36 shows high annotational agreement yields high evaluation scores, with stricter crowd evaluations and significant validity increase after four annotations.
Majority class annotation percentage positively influences evaluation scores except 100% agreement, where reduced total annotations and specific percentages matter.
In emotion annotations, Figure FIGREF36 shows crowd and experts follow similar patterns, with anticipation and joy equal and intensifiers and negators higher from the crowd.
The final graph in Figure FIGREF36 shows subclass agreement negatively correlates with evaluation scores, with three subclasses not affecting scores.
Evaluation scores improve after four annotations, subclass agreement negatively affects three or more subclasses, and the crowd is stricter, cheaper, and more scalable than experts.
Evaluation of intensifiers and negators used 541 PEL term groups with at least one intensifying subclass annotation, expecting relatively low evaluation scores.
Figure FIGREF40 defines low, mid, and high agreement levels for validity of the intensifying class for experts and the crowd.
Experts are far stricter than the crowd for intensifiers and negators, with differences over 40% at low agreement and 5.33% at high agreement.
Lexicon acquisition mixes subjective emotion annotation with objective linguistic element annotation, and the presented novel work flow provides quality results for both.
Subcomponents of lexicon acquisition could be improved individually, including spell check, filtering, and evaluation process.
Crowd diversity in annotation and evaluation is a limiting factor because fixed individuals annotating and evaluating the whole corpus would be preferred.
The corpus may limit term groups to domain-specific subjects, with NRC BIBREF21 showing 40% common terms and annotations increasing from 2.3 to 3.2.
The crowd can produce and evaluate a quality pure emotion lexicon without gold standards, though spam is common and post-annotation quality assessment should be implemented.
Workers labeled term groups as emotion, intensifiers, and stop words, with up to three emotions valid and intensifiers and negators hardest.
Stemming reduced costs by 45%, multi-emotion classification was lower than 10%, and minimal instructions worked best in tested interface designs.
The crowd is as capable as experts at evaluating lexicons, with strictness varying by emotional or linguistic evaluations and number of evaluators.
Future work includes a voluntary platform, Crowd4U or similar platforms, qualitative analysis of intensifiers and negators, and extending the approach to other linguistic elements.
Beyond polarity sentiment analysis can enhance simple polarity based applications, including marketing, politics, health monitoring, online social networks, and evaluation processes.
This work was supported by the EU project "QROWD - Because Big Data Integration is Humanly Possible".
